title: Quiz 13 — Mapping
text:
Spatial data and coordinate systems

1. (T/F) An sf object is basically a normal data frame with an extra geometry column.
True / False


2. (MC) Plain longitude/latitude coordinates (what GPS and most CSVs use) correspond to which CRS?
a. EPSG:3857 b. EPSG:4326 c. EPSG:5070 d. There is no CRS for lat/long


3. (MC) The CRS (coordinate reference system) of a spatial dataset is:
a. The rulebook that says what the coordinate numbers actually mean on the Earth
b. The number of rows in the data
c. The color scale of the map
d. The file format


4. (MC) A “choropleth” is:
a. A single location, like one sighting
b. A map that shades areas by a value
c. The rulebook for what coordinate numbers mean
d. An area outline, like a state


5. (T/F) ★ coord_sf(crs = 5070) reprojects the map for display only — it does not change your underlying data.
True / False

title: Quiz 13 — Mapping
text:
Making points spatial

6. (MC) Which call turns bigfoot_df into an sf object with CRS 4326?
a. st_as_sf(bigfoot_df, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
b. st_as_sf(bigfoot_df, coords = c("latitude", "longitude"), crs = 4326)
c. as_sf(bigfoot_df, lat, long)
d. st_as_sf(bigfoot_df)


7. (Fix) A student’s points land in the wrong hemisphere. Their call is st_as_sf(coords = c("latitude", "longitude"), crs = 4326). What is wrong?
a. coords must be x first, then y: c("longitude", "latitude")
b. crs should be 3857
c. st_as_sf() cannot take a crs argument
d. Nothing — the points are fine


8. (Fix) st_as_sf() errors because a few latitude values are NA. What must you do first?
a. filter(!is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude)) before st_as_sf()
b. Replace every NA with 0
c. Change the CRS
d. Use pivot_longer() first


9. (T/F) Latitude is the y-coordinate and longitude is the x-coordinate.
True / False

title: Quiz 13 — Mapping
text:
Drawing maps and choropleths

10. (MC) To draw states_sf as a grey basemap with bigfoot_sf points on top, the layer order is:
a. geom_sf(data = states_sf, ...) first, then geom_sf(data = bigfoot_sf, ...)
b. Points first, then the basemap on top
c. Order does not matter for maps
d. Both must be in a single geom_sf() call


11. (MC) A per-state choropleth of counts is built by:
a. Plotting points only
b. Counting per state, joining those counts to the state polygons, and filling by the count
c. Using pivot_wider() on the coordinates
d. Changing the CRS to 3857


12. (Predict) You join sighting counts to states_sf but the whole choropleth is grey with all-NA fills. The report state values are "Washington"; the map’s are "washington". Cause and fix?
a. Key mismatch from letter case; fix with str_to_lower() so both keys match
b. The CRS is wrong; change to 5070
c. geom_sf() is broken; use geom_polygon()
d. There are too many states


13. (Predict) ★ A choropleth of raw sighting counts (not per-capita) mostly ends up highlighting:
a. The states where the phenomenon is genuinely most common
b. The most populous states, because more people means more reports
c. The states with the smallest area
d. Nothing — counts cannot be mapped


14. (Fix) geom_sf(data = bigfoot_df) errors. bigfoot_df is a plain data frame with longitude/latitude columns. What is missing?
a. Convert it to an sf object first with st_as_sf(..., coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
b. geom_sf() should be geom_point()
c. You need library(ggplot2)
d. Nothing — this works

title: Quiz 11 — One-Way ANOVA
text:
Why ANOVA, and the F-statistic

1. (MC) The ANOVA F-statistic is a ratio of:
a. within-group variance / between-group variance
b. between-group variance / within-group variance (signal / noise)
c. the largest group mean / the smallest
d. sample size / number of groups


2. (T/F) Running three separate t-tests to compare three groups pushes the overall (family-wise) false-positive rate above 0.05.
True / False


3. (MC) With 4 groups, how many pairwise t-tests would you need to compare every pair?
a. 3 b. 4 c. 6 d. 12


4. (MC) “Between-group variance” in a penguin body-mass ANOVA means:
a. How much individual penguins scatter within their own species
b. How far apart the three species means are
c. The measurement error of the scale
d. The number of species


5. (MC) “Within-group variance” means:
a. How far apart the species means are
b. How much individual penguins scatter around their own species’ mean
c. The total number of penguins
d. The difference between the heaviest and lightest species

title: Quiz 11 — One-Way ANOVA
text:
The model

6. (MC) In lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_df):
a. body_mass_g is the predictor and species is the response
b. species is the predictor and body_mass_g is the response
c. Both variables are predictors
d. Invalid — species must be numeric


7. (Fix) A student writes lm(species ~ body_mass_g, data = penguins_df) to test whether mass differs by species. What is wrong?
a. The formula is backwards — it should be lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_df)
b. lm() cannot be used for ANOVA
c. penguins_df must be a matrix
d. Nothing is wrong


8. (MC) Why does the lecture prefer car::Anova(model, type = "II") over base anova(model) for the penguin data?
a. Anova() runs faster
b. The groups are unbalanced (different n per species), and Type II does not depend on variable order
c. anova() cannot handle a categorical predictor
d. Anova() automatically drops missing data


9. (Fix) Anova(mass_model, type = "II") errors with could not find function "Anova". Why?
a. library(car) was never loaded — capital Anova() lives in car
b. type must be "2"
c. mass_model is not a model
d. Anova() only works on two-way designs


10. (Fix) car::Anova(mass_model, type = "2") misbehaves. What is wrong with the type argument?
a. type must be a Roman numeral string: "I", "II", or "III"
b. type must be a number without quotes: 2
c. type should be "two"
d. Nothing — "2" is fine


11. (T/F) ★ With one predictor, Type I, II, and III ANOVA give the same F and p — but the lecture still builds the type = "II" habit now because the sums-of-squares type changes the answer once you have two or more (unbalanced) predictors.
True / False

title: Quiz 11 — One-Way ANOVA
text:
Assumptions

12. (MC) The three assumptions of a one-way ANOVA are:
a. Independence, normality of residuals, equal variance across groups
b. Linearity, large sample, no outliers
c. Equal group sizes, integer data, no missing values
d. Random slope, random intercept, nesting


13. (MC) shapiro.test(residuals(mass_model)) checks:
a. Equal variance across species
b. Normality of the model’s residuals
c. Whether the F-test is significant
d. Which species differ


14. (Fix) shapiro.test(mass_model) runs but does not check what the student thinks. What is wrong?
a. It is being run on the model object, not its residuals; use shapiro.test(residuals(mass_model))
b. shapiro.test() needs a formula
c. It should be leveneTest()
d. Nothing is wrong


15. (Fix) leveneTest(species ~ body_mass_g, data = penguins_df) is written backwards. What should it be?
a. leveneTest(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_df) — numeric response ~ grouping factor
b. leveneTest(penguins_df$species)
c. leveneTest(body_mass_g + species)
d. It is already correct


16. (Predict) leveneTest(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_df) returns p = 0.34. You:
a. Switch to Welch’s ANOVA — the variances differ
b. Proceed with the classic ANOVA — the variances are not significantly different
c. Stop — ANOVA is not valid
d. Run a t-test instead


17. (Fix) A student fits the model on penguins (raw) instead of penguins_df (cleaned). What is the risk?
a. None — lm() handles it identically
b. Rows with missing body_mass_g/species are silently dropped, so counts and plots may not match the model; the lecture drops NA explicitly for a clean, documented dataset
c. lm() will refuse to run
d. The species names change


18. (T/F) ★ With ~340 penguins, Shapiro-Wilk can flag tiny, harmless departures from normality as “significant,” so you should trust the Q-Q plot more in that situation.
True / False

title: Quiz 11 — One-Way ANOVA
text:
Predicting output

19. (Predict) penguins_df %>% count(species) prints:
a. 1 row, 1 column
b. 3 rows (Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo) with columns species and n
c. 342 rows
d. A single number


20. (Predict) A boxplot of body_mass_g by species with jittered points looks like:
a. One box for all penguins combined
b. Three boxes; Gentoo clearly higher/heavier than Adelie and Chinstrap, which overlap more with each other
c. A scatterplot with a trend line
d. A histogram


21. (Predict) par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(mass_model) produces, in order:
a. Residuals vs Fitted, Normal Q-Q, Scale-Location, Residuals vs Leverage
b. Histogram, boxplot, scatterplot, bar chart
c. Four identical scatterplots
d. The ANOVA table four times


22. (Predict) The ANOVA Pr(>F) comes back far below 0.001. What can you conclude?
a. All three species differ from each other
b. At least one species mean differs from the others — but not which ones
c. Gentoo is the heaviest
d. The residuals are normal


23. (Predict) mass_emm <- emmeans(mass_model, pairwise ~ species) then mass_emm$contrasts is printed. How many rows?
a. 1 b. 2 c. 3 (Adelie–Chinstrap, Adelie–Gentoo, Chinstrap–Gentoo) d. 9


24. (Predict) A means plot has one point per species and error bars showing the 95% CI of each estimated mean. Two error bars that overlap a lot would suggest:
a. Those two species’ means are not clearly distinguishable
b. Those two species definitely differ
c. The model failed
d. The sample size is too large

title: Quiz 11 — One-Way ANOVA
text:
Post-hoc: emmeans and compact letters

25. (MC) emmeans(model, pairwise ~ species) is used to:
a. Test equal variance across groups
b. Give the classic ANOVA F table
c. Run post-hoc pairwise comparisons (which groups differ)
d. Test normality of the residuals


26. (T/F) Tukey-adjusted emmeans pairwise comparisons already correct for multiple comparisons, so the family-wise error rate stays at 0.05 without extra work.
True / False


27. (Fix) mass_emm <- emmeans(mass_model, ~ species) then mass_emm$contrasts fails. What was forgotten?
a. pairwise ~ species — without pairwise, emmeans() returns only estimated means, no $contrasts
b. library(emmeans)
c. data = penguins_df
d. type = "II"


28. (Fix) multcomp::cld(mass_emm, Letters = letters) errors. What should be passed instead?
a. mass_emm$emmeans — cld() needs the emmeans grid, not the whole list
b. mass_model
c. penguins_df
d. residuals(mass_model)


29. (MC) A compact letter display assigns Adelie → “a”, Chinstrap → “a”, Gentoo → “b”. This means:
a. All three species differ
b. Adelie and Chinstrap do not differ; Gentoo differs from both
c. No species differ
d. Gentoo is missing data

title: Quiz 11 — One-Way ANOVA
text:
Hypotheses and reporting

30. (MC) H₀ and Hₐ for a one-way ANOVA on penguin body mass are:
a. H₀: μ_Adelie = μ_Chinstrap = μ_Gentoo ; Hₐ: at least one species mean differs
b. H₀: all species means differ ; Hₐ: all species means are equal
c. H₀: the residuals are normal ; Hₐ: they are not
d. H₀: Gentoo is heaviest ; Hₐ: Gentoo is lightest


31. (MC) Which is a prediction, not a hypothesis?
a. H₀: all three species means are equal
b. Hₐ: at least one species mean differs
c. “I expect Gentoo will be the heaviest because they look bigger”
d. α = 0.05


32. (MC) The ANOVA gives p < 0.001. Without a post-hoc test, you cannot conclude:
a. That at least one species mean differs
b. Which specific species differ from each other
c. That the F-statistic is large
d. That the result is unlikely under H₀


33. (T/F) A significant ANOVA F-test tells you that the groups differ, not which ones.
True / False


34. (MC) Which is a correctly formatted ANOVA results sentence?
a. “Body mass differed significantly among the three penguin species (one-way ANOVA: F(2, 339) = 343.6, p < 0.001). Tukey-adjusted comparisons showed all three species differed except Adelie and Chinstrap, with Gentoo heaviest.”
b. “The ANOVA was significant, p = 0.000, so Gentoo is heaviest.”
c. “There was a difference (F = 343.6).”
d. “p < 0.001 proves the species are different everywhere.”

title: Quiz 09 — Pivoting Real Data
text:
Wide vs. long (tidy) data

1. (T/F) ggplot() and group_by() generally need data in long (tidy) format, not wide.
True / False


2. (MC) A file has one row per day and one column per year (53 year-columns). To plot ice cover over time you first:
a. pivot_wider() the years into more columns
b. pivot_longer() the year-columns into a single year column
c. filter() out the years
d. arrange() by year


3. (T/F) You cannot group_by(year) on wide data with one column per year, because there is no year column to group by yet.
True / False


4. (T/F) “Tidy” data means every variable is its own column and every observation is its own row.
True / False

title: Quiz 09 — Pivoting Real Data
text:
pivot_longer() and pivot_wider()

5. (MC) pivot_longer() is used to:
a. Turn many columns into two key–value columns (tidy it)
b. Make a human-readable summary table
c. Keep the highest-value row per group
d. Split the data into groups


6. (MC) pivot_wider() is used to:
a. Turn many columns into key–value pairs
b. Spread tidy data back out into a wide, human-readable table
c. Drop missing values
d. Sort rows high to low


7. (Predict) ice_raw has 190 rows and 53 year-columns plus a date column. After pivot_longer(cols = -date), the result is about:
a. 3 columns, ~10,000 rows
b. 53 columns, 190 rows
c. 2 columns, 243 rows
d. Unchanged


8. (Predict) pivot_wider(id_cols = year, names_from = month, values_from = ice_cover) produces:
a. One row per month, one column per year
b. One row per year, one column per month
c. A single column
d. The same shape as the input


9. (Fix) ice_raw %>% pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "year") errors with Column 'date' doesn't exist. The day labels are still row names. What is missing?
a. rownames_to_column(var = "date") before the pivot
b. library(tidyr)
c. A values_to argument
d. arrange(date)


10. (Fix) ★ After pivot_longer() the new year column holds values like "X1998" instead of 1998. Which argument strips the leading "X"?
a. names_prefix = "X"
b. values_drop_na = TRUE
c. names_sep = "X"
d. cols = -X

title: Quiz 09 — Pivoting Real Data
text:
slice_max() and reading messy files

11. (MC) To keep, for each year, the single row with the highest ice_cover, you use:
a. group_by(year) %>% slice_max(order_by = ice_cover, n = 1)
b. filter(ice_cover == max)
c. arrange(ice_cover) %>% head(1)
d. pivot_wider(ice_cover)


12. (T/F) slice_max(n = 1) without group_by() first returns the single highest row in the whole data set, not one per group.
True / False


13. (MC) ★ A NOAA text file is space-separated, not comma-separated. Which is true?
a. read_csv() is fine — it auto-detects any separator
b. Use read_table() / read_delim(); read_csv() expects commas and would misparse it
c. You must open it in Excel first
d. Space-separated files cannot be read into R


14. (Fix) read_csv("data/noaa_ice.txt") reads the whole file into a single column. Why?
a. The file is space/tab-separated, not comma-separated; use a reader that matches the delimiter
b. .txt files cannot be read
c. You need library(readr)
d. The file is empty

title: Quiz 07 — Downloading and Summarizing Weather Data
Quiz 07 — Downloading and Summarizing Weather Data
text:
Downloading the data

1. (MC) Which function and package downloaded the Duluth record into R?
a. read_csv() from readr
b. get_GSOD() from GSODR
c. download.file() from base R
d. import() from rio


2. (MC) Why do we run select() right after downloading the raw weather data?
a. select() is required before ggplot() will run
b. get_GSOD() returns 40+ columns and we only need a handful
c. select() converts daily data to yearly
d. R will not store the object otherwise


3. (MC) dlh_temp_df %>% select(temp) errors even though a temperature column exists. Why?
a. select() cannot take one column
b. The column is named TEMP (uppercase) — R is case-sensitive
c. You need library(GSODR)
d. temp is a reserved word


4. (Fix) dlh_temp_df %>% select(temp, YEAR, MONTH) errors with Column 'temp' doesn't exist. How do you find the right name?
a. Run names(dlh_temp_df) and use the exact (uppercase) name: select(TEMP, YEAR, MONTH)
b. Reinstall GSODR
c. Use filter() instead of select()
d. Add quotes: select("temp")


5. (MC) The difference between YEARMODA and the separate YEAR, MONTH, DAY columns is:
a. YEARMODA is one combined date value (good for a time axis); YEAR/MONTH/DAY are the same date split into three numbers (good for group_by())
b. They hold completely different dates
c. YEARMODA is text and the others are dates
d. There is no difference

title: Quiz 07 — Downloading and Summarizing Weather Data
text:
Summarizing over time

6. (T/F) Summarizing daily data to yearly means “loses information” in a bad way and makes the analysis weaker.
True / False


7. (Predict) dlh_temp_df has ~28,000 daily rows (1948–2025). After group_by(YEAR) %>% summarize(TEMP = mean(TEMP, na.rm = TRUE)), the result has about:
a. 28,000 rows b. 78 rows (one per year) c. 12 rows d. 1 row


8. (T/F) mean(TEMP) returns NA for a year if any single day that year is missing; mean(TEMP, na.rm = TRUE) fixes it.
True / False


9. (Fix) This returns NA for every year. What is missing?
dlh_temp_df %>%
  group_by(YEAR) %>%
  summarize(TEMP = mean(TEMP))
a. na.rm = TRUE inside mean()
b. arrange(YEAR) before summarize()
c. A library() call
d. Nothing — this is correct


10. (Predict) A scatter of ~28,000 raw daily TEMP values against YEARMODA looks like:
a. A clean straight line showing the warming trend
b. A dense band dominated by the yearly seasonal cycle, with no long-term trend visible by eye
c. A single point
d. A U-shaped curve


11. (Predict) Compared with the raw daily plot, the yearly-means plot (one point per year) with an lm smooth shows:
a. Even more seasonal noise
b. The seasonal noise averaged out, so a clear overall warming trend line is visible
c. Exactly the same thing
d. Nothing — 78 points is too few to plot

title: Quiz 07 — Downloading and Summarizing Weather Data
text:
Modeling the trend with lm()

12. (MC) In lm(TEMP ~ YEAR, data = dlh_year_df), which is the response and which is the predictor?
a. YEAR is the response, TEMP is the predictor
b. TEMP is the response, YEAR is the predictor
c. Both are predictors
d. Both are responses


13. (MC) To get the rate of warming per year from yearly_temp_model, you extract:
a. coef(yearly_temp_model)[1] — the intercept
b. coef(yearly_temp_model)[2] — the slope
c. summary(yearly_temp_model)$r.squared
d. residuals(yearly_temp_model)


14. (Fix) A student wants the warming rate but writes this. What did they extract?
yearly_temp_model <- lm(TEMP ~ YEAR, data = dlh_year_df)
warming_rate <- coef(yearly_temp_model)[1]
a. They grabbed the intercept; use coef(yearly_temp_model)[2] for the slope
b. They grabbed the slope; that is correct
c. coef() should be resid()
d. [1] should be ["YEAR"] — same thing, no bug


15. (Predict) lm(TEMP ~ YEAR, data = dlh_year_df) gives a slope of 0.025 with p < 0.001. The one-sentence conclusion is:
a. There is no evidence of a trend
b. Duluth’s annual mean temperature is rising at a statistically significant rate (~0.25 °C/decade)
c. Every year is exactly 0.025 °C warmer with no uncertainty
d. The model failed to converge


16. (T/F) A yearly slope of 0.02 °C/year is trivial and cannot represent a meaningful long-term change.
True / False


17. (T/F) Multiplying a yearly warming slope by 10 converts it to °C per decade.
True / False


18. (T/F) ★ A yearly temperature time series can violate the independence assumption of lm() because a warm year tends to be followed by another warm year (autocorrelation).
True / False


19. (MC) ★ A student fits the trend model directly on the ~28,000 daily rows. It runs without error. What is the problem?
daily_trend_model <- lm(TEMP ~ YEARMODA, data = dlh_temp_df)
a. There is no problem — more rows is always better
b. Each row is still one day, so the residuals still carry the huge seasonal swing (~30 °C) that is not the signal of interest; the yearly summary removes that noise first
c. lm() cannot handle a date column
d. YEARMODA must be YEAR

title: Quiz 07 — Downloading and Summarizing Weather Data
text:
case_when() and seasons

20. (MC) case_when() comes from which package (part of the tidyverse)?
a. GSODR b. dplyr c. ggplot2 d. lubridate


21. (Fix) Every row comes back NA for season. What is wrong?
dlh_temp_df %>%
  mutate(season = case_when(
    MONTH == c(6, 7, 8) ~ "summer",
    TRUE ~ "other"
  ))
a. case_when() cannot make text
b. MONTH == c(6, 7, 8) compares element-by-element; use MONTH %in% c(6, 7, 8)
c. TRUE ~ "other" must come first
d. mutate() should be summarize()


22. (Fix) This is meant to keep only summer and winter rows but silently keeps every row. What is wrong?
season_year_df <- dlh_season_df %>%
  filter(season == c("summer", "winter"))
a. filter() needs group_by() first
b. season == c("summer", "winter") compares element-wise; use season %in% c("summer", "winter")
c. The strings need to be capitalized
d. filter() should be select()


23. (Predict) Seasons are defined as summer = 3 months, winter = 3 months, shoulder = the other 6. In count(season), which category has the most rows?
a. summer b. winter c. shoulder (about twice either single season) d. they are all equal

title: Quiz 07 — Downloading and Summarizing Weather Data
text:
Comparing seasons in a plot

24. (T/F) To split points by season in a ggplot, you need color = season inside aes().
True / False


25. (Fix) In season_temp_plot, every point is the same default color instead of split by season. What line is wrong or missing?
season_year_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = YEAR, y = TEMP)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
a. color = season is missing from aes()
b. geom_point() should be geom_line()
c. method = "lm" should be method = "loess"
d. You need facet_wrap(~season)


26. (MC) In a plot with a separate geom_smooth(method = "lm") line per season, how do you tell which season is warming faster?
a. Whichever line starts higher on the y-axis
b. Whichever line is steeper (bigger slope)
c. Whichever line is a different color
d. Whichever season has more points

Applying it

27. (MC) Which of these is a prediction, not a hypothesis?
a. H₀: the slope of TEMP on YEAR is 0
b. Hₐ: the slope is not 0
c. “I expect Duluth has gotten warmer over the record”
d. α = 0.05


28. (MC) You reuse this workflow for a new city and station ID. Which is a sensible check before trusting the trend?
a. Assume the download is fine and skip straight to lm()
b. Use glimpse()/count() per year to check for big gaps or a too-short record before interpreting the slope
c. Delete every NA row without looking
d. Only trust the result if the slope is positive

title: Quiz 05 — Quarto and Markdown Reports
section: Why Quarto, and the parts of a .qmd
text:
Why Quarto, and the parts of a .qmd

1. (MC) Every .qmd file is built from three kinds of content. Which list is correct?
a. YAML front matter, Markdown text, code chunks
b. Title, abstract, references
c. Console, Script, Environment
d. Data, figures, tables


2. (MC) The YAML front matter at the top of a .qmd file is best described as:
a. A code chunk that runs first
b. The “recipe” — settings like title, author, and output format
c. Where you write your discussion section
d. Decoration with no effect on rendering


3. (T/F) A Quarto report is more reproducible than a script whose numbers are copy-pasted into Word by hand, because it recomputes every number and figure from the data on each render.
True / False


4. (T/F) A number typed by hand into your prose stays correct automatically when the underlying data changes.
True / False

title: Quiz 05 — Quarto and Markdown Reports
text:
YAML

5. (T/F) YAML is space-sensitive: a stray leading space or a mix of tabs and spaces can stop the file from rendering.
True / False


6. (Fix) This YAML fails to parse. What is wrong?
---
title: "Leaf Report"
author: "Your Name"
 date: today
format: docx
---
a. date: today has a stray leading space, breaking the alignment of the top-level keys
b. title cannot have quotes
c. format: docx must be format: word
d. author must come before title


7. (Fix) This YAML line causes a parse error: format:docx. What is wrong?
a. docx should be capitalized
b. There must be a space after the colon: format: docx
c. format is not a real YAML key
d. It needs quotes: format:"docx"


8. (Predict) Given this YAML, what will the Word document have?
format:
  docx:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
a. A table of contents and numbered section headings
b. No table of contents, unnumbered sections
c. A PowerPoint file
d. Nothing changes from the default


9. (Predict) Given this YAML, how many output files does one Render produce?
format:
  docx: default
  html: default
  pptx: default
a. 1 b. 2 c. 3 d. it errors — you can only list one


10. (T/F) You can produce a Word document, a web page, and slides from one .qmd by listing docx, html, and pptx under format: and rendering once.
True / False

title: Quiz 05 — Quarto and Markdown Reports
text:
Markdown

11. (MC) In Markdown, what does a single # at the start of a line do?
a. Comments out the line
b. Makes a top-level heading
c. Makes a bullet point
d. Makes the text bold


12. (Predict) How does this Markdown render?
# Introduction

We measured leaf mass on the **sunny** and **shady** sides.

- Null hypothesis: no difference
- Alternate hypothesis: sides differ
a. All four lines as plain text
b. “Introduction” as a big heading, “sunny”/“shady” bold, and the last two lines as bullets
c. Everything as a bulleted list
d. “Introduction” as a bullet and the rest as headings


13. (MC) Surrounding a word with **double asterisks** makes it:
a. italic b. bold c. a heading d. code

title: Quiz 05 — Quarto and Markdown Reports
text:
Code chunks and chunk options

14. (MC) Which fence correctly opens a chunk that runs as R code?
a. ### {r}
b. ```{r}
c. [[r]]
d. <r>


15. (MC) echo and eval control, respectively:
a. Whether the code is shown; whether the code runs
b. Whether the code runs; whether the code is shown
c. The font size; the figure size
d. The output format; the file name


16. (Predict) A chunk has echo: false and eval: true. In the rendered document you see:
a. The code only
b. The result only
c. Both the code and the result
d. Neither


17. (Predict) A chunk has echo: true and eval: false. In the rendered document you see:
a. The code only (nothing runs, so no output)
b. The result only
c. Both
d. Neither


18. (Predict) This chunk has echo: false and eval: true:
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
mean(c(4, 3, 5, 8))
What appears in the rendered document?
a. The code and the number 5
b. Just the number 5
c. Just the code
d. An error


19. (T/F) echo: true, eval: false is a useful combination for a student workbook: learners see the exact code without it running.
True / False


20. (MC) A situation where you would set echo: false in a chunk:
a. A polished lab report for a reader who wants results, not code
b. A teaching handout where students must see the code
c. Any time the code has an error
d. Never — echo should always be true

title: Quiz 05 — Quarto and Markdown Reports
text:
Inline code and cross-references

21. (MC) “Inline code” means:
a. A whole code chunk on its own line
b. A small live R expression dropped into a sentence so the value updates on every render
c. Code that has been commented out
d. Code written in the Console instead of the document


22. (Predict) An earlier chunk computed mean_shady <- 7.8. You write “Shady-side leaves averaged” then an inline code expression that calls mean_shady, then ” g.” When the document renders, the sentence reads:
a. Shady-side leaves averaged mean_shady g.
b. Shady-side leaves averaged 7.8 g.
c. Shady-side leaves averaged (the raw expression text, unevaluated) g.
d. An error


23. (T/F) ★ For a figure cross-reference like @fig-leaf-plot to work, the chunk’s label must begin with fig-.
True / False

title: Quiz 05 — Quarto and Markdown Reports
text:
Troubleshooting a render

24. (T/F) Quarto runs the code chunks top to bottom in a fresh session, so a chunk that loads your libraries and data must appear above any chunk that uses them.
True / False


25. (T/F) Two code chunks in the same document are allowed to share the same label.
True / False


26. (Fix) Render fails with Duplicate chunk label 'plot'. Two chunks are labeled #| label: plot. The fix is:
a. Delete one of the chunks
b. Give each chunk a unique label, e.g. plot-box and plot-means
c. Remove all labels from the document
d. Change the format to html


27. (Fix) A chunk errors with object 'leaf_df' not found. Most likely cause?
a. leaf_df is spelled wrong everywhere
b. The chunk that reads in leaf_df is missing or is below this chunk
c. Quarto cannot use data frames
d. You must render to Word first


28. (Fix) A chunk errors with could not find function "%>%". The fix is:
a. Add library(tidyverse) in a chunk near the top, before any chunk that uses the pipe
b. Replace every %>% with a comma
c. Render to html instead of docx
d. Rename the chunk


29. (Fix) An inline value renders literally as the raw expression text instead of a number. The prose refers to maen_shady, but the earlier chunk created mean_shady. What is wrong?
a. Inline code cannot use objects from other chunks
b. The object name is misspelled — maen_shady should be mean_shady
c. You must render to PowerPoint
d. The chunk needs echo: true


30. (Fix) ★ Rendering stops partway through with no clear line number. A student’s R chunk opens with the fence line ```{r summary-table} and has three lines of code, but the student never typed the closing ``` fence line after the code. The problem is:
a. The closing ``` fence is missing, so Quarto treats the rest of the file as still inside the chunk
b. group_by() must come after summarize()
c. The chunk label has a dash in it
d. na.rm = TRUE is invalid

title: Quiz 03 — Wrangling and Summary Statistics
text:
The pipe %>%

1. (MC) What does the pipe %>% do?
a. Assigns a value to a variable
b. Takes the result on its left and feeds it in as the first argument on its right
c. Compares two values for equality
d. Loads a package


2. (T/F) Writing one pipeline with %>% runs the steps top to bottom, which is easier to read than nesting the same functions inside each other.
True / False


3. (Fix) mass_g %>% mean(leaf_df) errors. What is the correct call?
a. leaf_df %>% pull(mass_g) %>% mean(na.rm = TRUE)
b. mean(leaf_df) %>% mass_g
c. leaf_df %>% mean(mass_g)
d. mass_g %>% leaf_df %>% mean()

title: Quiz 03 — Wrangling and Summary Statistics
section: The core verbs: filter, select, mutate, arrange, summarize
text:
The core verbs: filter, select, mutate, arrange, summarize

4. (MC) filter() is used to:
a. Keep only certain columns
b. Keep only rows that meet a condition
c. Sort the rows
d. Add a new column


5. (MC) select() is used to:
a. Keep only certain columns
b. Keep only rows that meet a condition
c. Collapse the data to one summary row
d. Rename the data frame


6. (MC) mutate() is used to:
a. Delete rows
b. Add a new column (or overwrite an existing one)
c. Sort rows from high to low
d. Count missing values


7. (MC) summarize() is used to:
a. Keep matching rows
b. Collapse many rows into a summary such as a mean or a count
c. Reorder the columns
d. Load the tidyverse


8. (MC) arrange(desc(mass_g)) sorts the rows so that:
a. The lightest leaf is first
b. The heaviest leaf is first
c. The rows are shuffled randomly
d. Only sunny leaves are kept


9. (T/F) By default mutate() keeps every existing column and adds the new one alongside them.
True / False


10. (Predict) How many columns does the result have?
leaf_df %>%
  select(shade, mass_g) %>%
  mutate(mass_mg = mass_g * 1000)
a. 1 b. 2 c. 3 d. 8


11. (Predict) leaf_df has 24 rows (12 sunny, 12 shady). Roughly how many rows does leaf_df %>% filter(shade == "sunny") return?
a. 0 b. 12 c. 24 d. 48


12. (Predict) Reading top to bottom, what does this pipeline do?
clean_df <- leaf_df %>%
  filter(mass_g > 0) %>%
  select(shade, mass_g, thickness_mm) %>%
  arrange(shade, desc(mass_g))
a. Adds three new columns, then deletes rows
b. Keeps rows with mass_g > 0, keeps three columns, then sorts by shade and (within shade) by mass_g high to low
c. Groups by shade and computes a mean
d. Sorts first, then filters, then renames

title: Quiz 03 — Wrangling and Summary Statistics
text:
= vs == and case sensitivity

13. (MC) Inside filter(), which symbol tests whether two things are equal?
a. = b. == c. <- d. %>%


14. (Fix) This throws We detected a named input. What is the fix?
leaf_df %>% filter(shade = "sunny")
a. filter(shade == "sunny") — use == to compare, not =
b. filter("sunny" = shade)
c. filter(shade <- "sunny")
d. filter(shade = "sunny", strict = FALSE)


15. (Fix) The student typed "Sunny" but got zero rows even though sunny leaves exist. Why?
leaf_df %>% filter(shade == "Sunny")
a. filter() only works on numbers
b. R is case-sensitive; the data stores "sunny" (lowercase)
c. You need quotes around shade
d. filter() must come before the pipe


16. (T/F) filter(shade == "Sunny") and filter(shade == "sunny") return the same rows.
True / False

title: Quiz 03 — Wrangling and Summary Statistics
text:
Missing values (NA)

17. (MC) x has five values, two of which are NA. Which counts only the real (non-missing) values?
a. length(x)
b. sum(!is.na(x))
c. nrow(x)
d. mean(x)


18. (T/F) mean(x) returns NA if even one value in x is NA, unless you add na.rm = TRUE.
True / False


19. (Predict) What does the second line print?
x <- c(4, 3, NA, 7, NA)
sum(!is.na(x))
a. 2 b. 3 c. 5 d. NA


20. (Fix) This returns NA with no error message. Why, and what is the fix?
mean(leaf_df$paper_mass_g)
a. paper_mass_g has missing values; add na.rm = TRUE
b. mean() does not work on data frames
c. You forgot library(dplyr)
d. The column name is misspelled


21. (Fix) ★ This SE line is silently wrong when sunny_mass contains NA values. What is the bug?
se_sunny <- sd(sunny_mass, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(length(sunny_mass))
a. sd() should be var()
b. length(sunny_mass) counts the NA values too; use sum(!is.na(sunny_mass))
c. sqrt() should be ^2
d. Nothing is wrong

title: Quiz 03 — Wrangling and Summary Statistics
text:
Mean, median, SD, SE

22. (Predict) Sunny masses are 5, 6, 7, 8, 50. What are the mean and the median?
a. mean = 7, median = 15.2
b. mean = 15.2, median = 7
c. mean = 7, median = 7
d. mean = 50, median = 8


23. (MC) For the data in Q22 (5, 6, 7, 8, 50), which is the “fairer” summary of a typical value?
a. The mean, because it uses every value
b. The median, because the single large value (50) drags the mean away from the bulk of the data
c. They are equally fair here
d. Neither — you must remove all five values


24. (T/F) SD describes how spread out the individual data points are; SE describes how precisely you have estimated the group mean.
True / False


25. (T/F) Because SE = SD / √n, collecting more leaves per group makes the SE smaller.
True / False


26. (T/F) ★ If a group’s mean is much larger than its median, that usually points to a right-skewed distribution — a few unusually large values pulling the mean up.
True / False

title: Quiz 03 — Wrangling and Summary Statistics
text:
group_by() + summarize()

27. (Predict) How many rows does stats_df have?
stats_df <- leaf_df %>%
  group_by(shade) %>%
  summarize(mean_mass = mean(mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
a. 1 b. 2 c. 12 d. 24


28. (MC) group_by(shade) %>% summarize(...) gives one row of statistics per:
a. leaf
b. level of shade (so: sunny, shady)
c. column
d. whole data set


29. (Predict) Describe the shape of this result:
leaf_df %>%
  group_by(shade) %>%
  summarize(n = sum(!is.na(mass_g)),
            mean_mass = mean(mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
a. 1 row, 2 columns
b. 2 rows, 3 columns (shade, n, mean_mass)
c. 24 rows, 3 columns
d. 3 rows, 2 columns

title: Quiz 03 — Wrangling and Summary Statistics
text:
Common mistakes

30. (Fix) The student expected size_class to appear when they check leaf_df afterward, but it is not there. Why?
leaf_df %>%
  mutate(size_class = if_else(mass_g > 0.5, "large", "small"))

names(leaf_df)
a. mutate() is broken
b. The result of mutate() was never assigned back (e.g. leaf_df <- leaf_df %>% mutate(...))
c. if_else() cannot make text
d. You need group_by() first


31. (T/F) A wrangling step like leaf_df %>% filter(mass_g > 0.5) changes leaf_df itself, even if you do not assign the result to anything.
True / False


32. (Fix) ★ The student wanted only mass_g and thickness_mm, but this keeps every column except those two. What happened?
leaf_df %>% select(-mass_g, -thickness_mm)
a. The minus signs tell select() to drop those columns; remove them: select(mass_g, thickness_mm)
b. select() needs quotes: select("-mass_g", "-thickness_mm")
c. select() should be filter()
d. Nothing is wrong — this keeps the two columns

title: Overview
text:
Data Science Course
Bill Perry
This course will serve as an introduction to reproducible data science and analysis using R. Specifically the goal is to introduce students to all facets of managing a research project with an emphasis on:

Developing questions fro observations, hypotheses, and predictions for testing statistically
Designing data workflows with data entry, curation, QA/QC, and cleaning
Using a controlled vocabulary and organized project structure and documenting the metadata for the project
Importing data into R and doing calculations and transformations
Visualizing data using ggplot
Understanding how to decide on statistical tests that are appropriate

-   Descriptive Statistics
-   T-Tests     
-   Regressions.    
-   Analysis of Variance.  
-   Analyzing Frequencies.   

In the main webpage I have provided links to all the information you will need:

links to readings that should be read prior to class
powerpoint lectures that should be reviewed prior to class
in-class activities that will actively cover the materials in the powerpoints

title: Lecture 05 — Wrangling Data
text:
Where we left off (Lecture 04 — GGPlot II)

Setup — R and Positron installed; project folders created (data/, figures/, scripts/)
Loading data — read_excel() and read_csv(); a first look with glimpse()
Pipe — %>% reads as “then”; chains steps together
GGPlot I & II — geoms, facets, stat_summary(), scale_color_manual(), coordinates, and themes







Note



✅ Key idea from Lecture 04
You can already load data and plot it beautifully. Today we learn to reshape and clean the data itself, before it ever reaches ggplot().




Goals for Today


The core tidyverse verbs:

filter() — pick rows by a condition
select() — pick columns by name
mutate() — create new columns
arrange() — sort rows
Chain them all into a pipeline







Tip



🖐 Try it yourself
By the end you will wrangle our leaf data into exactly the columns and rows you need, in one connected pipeline.



Our tools today:

readxl
tidyverse

References:

📖 R4DS Ch 3 — Data Transformation
📖 R4DS Ch 5 — Data Tidying
🌐 Data Carpentry

Naming conventions:

data frames → _df
plots → _plot
models → _model





How to Use These Slides — Predict · Type · Run


This is a shorter lecture than usual — one focused idea, wrangling, done properly. You will switch to the activity once, at the end, and type the code yourself into your R script there.
For every code block, do three things:

Predict — before it runs, say what you think the output will be
Type it out by hand — do not copy-paste
Run it and compare to your prediction








Note



✅ Why bother?

filter(), select(), mutate(), and arrange() look interchangeable on a slide — guessing the output first is what actually forces you to tell them apart.
You will type %>% dozens of times today; typing it now is what makes it automatic later, when you’re chaining five verbs under a deadline instead of reading one line calmly.







Load Libraries and Data

# Load all packages at the top of every script ----------
library(readxl) # reading Excel files
library(tidyverse) # data wrangling + ggplot2
library(janitor) # clean_names()


# Read the leaf data from the data folder ---------------
leaf_df <- read_excel("data/2026_09_03_data_sci_leaf_area.xlsx") %>%
  clean_names()



Take a First Look

# glimpse(): one row per column — name, type, first values
glimpse(leaf_df)

Rows: 53
Columns: 8
$ twig_id      <chr> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, "twig_1",…
$ leaf_id      <chr> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, "l07", "l…
$ teams        <chr> "12345", "12345", "12345", "12345", "12345", "12345", "12…
$ shade        <chr> "sunny", "sunny", "sunny", "sunny", "sunny", "sunny", "sh…
$ mass_g       <dbl> 0.4000, 0.4800, 0.3400, 0.6500, 0.2700, 0.4300, 0.3900, 0…
$ petiole_mm   <dbl> 79.0000, 63.0000, 68.0000, 35.0000, 34.0000, 40.0000, 40.…
$ thickness_mm <dbl> 0.15, 0.14, 0.14, 0.15, 0.11, 0.16, 0.14, 0.15, 0.12, 0.1…
$ paper_mass_g <dbl> 0.2100, 0.2100, 0.2100, 0.2400, 0.1500, 0.3400, 0.2900, 0…



<chr> = character (shade, teams)
<dbl> = numeric (mass_g, petiole_mm, thickness_mm, paper_mass_g)



The Core Tidyverse Verbs


Five functions do most of the work in data wrangling:



Function
What it does




filter()
keep rows matching a condition


select()
keep columns by name


mutate()
add or change a column


arrange()
sort rows


summarize()
collapse rows to a summary



All take a data frame as first input (via %>%) and return a data frame. We’ll wrangle with the first four today — summarize() is next lecture’s topic.
📖 R4DS §3 — Data Transformation







Note



✅ Why these five?
Almost every wrangling step you’ll write this semester decomposes into some combination of picking rows, picking columns, adding a column, sorting, or collapsing to a summary — that’s filter, select, mutate, arrange, and summarize.


Think of them as building blocks:
filter()   → rows you want
select()   → columns you want
mutate()   → new columns you need
arrange()  → order the rows
summarize()→ collapse to summaries (next lecture)

Common comparison operators:



Symbol
Meaning




==

!=

> <

>= <=

Warning

Live Demo — Watch It Break (on purpose)


I will type this wrong on purpose:
# One equals sign — a very common mistake
leaf_df %>% filter(shade = "sunny")
R stops and tells us:
Error in `filter()`:
! We detected a named input.
i This usually means that you've used `=` instead of `==`.
Now the fix — two equals signs:
leaf_df %>% filter(shade == "sunny")







Tip



✅ Why show a broken filter()?
filter(shade = "sunny") is the single most common typo in this whole unit, because = and == look almost identical and only one of them tests equality. dplyr’s error message actually names the mistake — “you’ve used = instead of ==” — so once you’ve seen it fixed here, the next time R prints it at you it’s a fix, not a mystery.

The Full Pipeline



# Chain all the verbs together -------------------------
# Read it top to bottom like a recipe

wrangled_df <- leaf_df %>%
  filter(mass_g > 0) %>% # remove any zeros
  select(shade, mass_g, thickness_mm) %>% # keep only needed cols
  mutate(
    mass_mg = mass_g * 1000,
    size_class = if_else(mass_g > 0.5, "large", "small")
  ) %>%
  arrange(shade, desc(mass_g)) # sort by shade, then mass

title: Lecture 07 — Real Climate Data in R
text:
Where we left off (Lecture 06)

Linear regression — fit a calibration curve (area ~ mass) with lm()
Reading summary() — slope b, intercept a, R², p-value for the slope
Least squares — the line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals
Assumption checks — residual vs. fitted plot, QQ plot, Shapiro-Wilk on residuals
predict() — confidence intervals (mean Y) vs. prediction intervals (one new Y)
Applied it — converted paper tracing mass into predicted leaf area (cm²)







Note



✅ Transition
So far every regression we have run used a dataset you were handed. Today we download real data from inside R for the first time — long-term weather records for Duluth, MN — and use that same regression toolkit to ask a much bigger question: is it getting warmer?




Goals for Today



Download real weather station data from inside R (no Excel step!)
Explore raw daily data — and see why raw data alone is hard to read
Summarize the same data by day, week, month, and year — and watch the story get clearer
Reuse lm() to estimate the rate of change (slope) in temperature over time
Use case_when() to build a new categorical variable — summer vs. winter
Compare how fast each season is warming







Tip



🖐 Try it yourself
By the end you’ll have downloaded a real NOAA climate record and estimated how many degrees per decade Duluth has warmed.



Tools today:

GSODR, tidyverse, lubridate

Textbook:

📖 R for Data Science 2e — Hadley Wickham

Ch. 3 Data transformation
Ch. 17 Dates and times

📖 Data Carpentry — R for Ecologists

Naming conventions:

data frames → _df
plots → _plot
models → _model





How to Use These Slides — Predict · Type · Run


This lecture runs in four short chunks. After each chunk you switch to the activity and type the code yourself.
For every code block, do three things:

Predict — before it runs, say what you think the output will be
Type it out by hand — do not copy-paste
Run it and compare to your prediction








Note



✅ Why bother? (the evidence)

Before get_GSOD() runs, guess the row count or the shape of the trend — that guess is what your brain checks the real output against.
Retyping group_by(YEAR, MONTH) instead of pasting it is what makes you notice you meant YEAR alone.
Downloading, then immediately summarizing in the same sitting, is what keeps the whole workflow — not just isolated commands — in your head.







🧩 Chunk 1 of 4 · Download & Explore Raw Data
We will cover: where GSOD data comes from, downloading it with get_GSOD(), trimming columns, and plotting the raw daily record.






Tip



🖐 After this chunk: Activity Parts 1–3 (download, trim, and raw-plot the Duluth data).




Where Does This Data Come From?


GSOD = Global Surface Summary of the Day, maintained by NOAA. It contains daily weather observations from thousands of stations worldwide, some going back to the 1940s.
The GSODR package lets us pull this data directly into R — no manual download, no Excel, no copy-paste.
The station we’ll use:

Duluth International Airport
Station ID 727450-14913
Daily records back to 1948 — 78 years of data


Why this matters:

This is the same kind of messy, real-world data you’ll meet in your own research
Today’s workflow — download → explore → summarize → model — is the same workflow you’ll use for your final project

📖 R4DS Ch. 3 — every analysis starts with getting data into R




Load Libraries and Download the Data

library(tidyverse) # data manipulation + ggplot2
library(GSODR) # download NOAA weather station data


# Download daily Duluth weather data, 1948-2025 --------
# this is DAILY data - rows = days, so expect ~28,000 rows
duluth_df <- get_GSOD(years = 1948:2025, station = "727450-14913")

years = 1948:2025 is a vector — shorthand for “every year in this range”
This download can take a minute — daily data for 78 years is a lot of rows!







Important



Don’t panic at the row count. Daily data for 78 years ≈ 28,000 rows. We will fix that with summarizing.






Trim to What We Need



# Keep only the columns we actually need -----------------
dlh_temp_df <- duluth_df %>%
  select(
    STNID,
    NAME,
    YEARMODA,
    YEAR,
    MONTH,
    DAY,
    TEMP,
    MXSPD,
    PRCP,
    I_SNOW_ICE
  )

Why select() here:

get_GSOD() returns 40+ columns — station metadata, multiple temperature scales, attribute flags
We only need a handful for this question
This is the same select() skill from Lecture 02 — applied to a much wider real-world file

📖 R4DS Ch. 3.2 — select() for picking columns




Live Demo — Watch It Break (on purpose)


NOAA’s column names are UPPERCASE. I’ll forget that:
# The column is TEMP, but I type temp
dlh_temp_df %>% select(temp)
R errors:
Error in `select()`:
! Can't select columns that don't exist.
✖ Column `temp` doesn't exist.
The fix — match the exact case:
dlh_temp_df %>% select(TEMP)   # names(dlh_temp_df) shows the real names







Tip



✅ Why show a broken run?
R is case-sensitive — temp ≠ TEMP. When a column “doesn’t exist,” run names(df) and check capitalization. Downloaded data rarely uses the names you’d guess.






First Look — Plot the Raw Daily Data






Note



🔮 Predict first: This plots ~28,000 daily points. Before you see it — will a long-term warming trend be visible, or will something else dominate the picture?





# Plot every single daily temperature ---------------------
raw_temp_plot <- dlh_temp_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = YEARMODA, y = TEMP)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.5) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Duluth Daily Mean Temperature, 1948–2025",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

raw_temp_plot









What do you see?

A dense, fuzzy band — the seasonal cycle (winter ↔︎ summer) dominates the plot
~28,000 points overlapping each other
Any long-term trend is completely hidden inside the seasonal noise

The problem: raw daily data shows you everything — which means it can hide the one thing you’re looking for.




🛑 Pause — Do Activity Parts 1–3 Now
Download the Duluth record with get_GSOD(), trim to the columns you need, and plot the raw daily temperatures. Predict what the raw plot will look like before you run it.


🧩 Chunk 2 of 4 · Summarize to Reveal the Trend
We will cover: why summarizing helps, and group_by() %>% summarize() at the monthly and yearly levels — watching the story get clearer.






Tip



🖐 After this chunk: Activity Parts 4–5 (summarize by month, then by year).




The Fix — Summarize the Story Out of the Noise


The idea: group the data into bigger time chunks, then take the mean within each chunk.



Summary level
group_by()
Rows after summary




Daily (raw)
none
~28,000


Monthly
YEAR, MONTH
~936


Yearly
YEAR
78



Each step trades detail for clarity. We lose day-to-day weather noise, but the climate signal becomes visible.

This is the same logic as Lecture 03’s group_by() + summarize() — just applied to time instead of to side (sunny/shady).






Tip



🖐 Try it yourself
Watch the same underlying data tell three different stories as we change the summary level.






Summarize by Month



# Mean temperature per year-month -----------------------
dlh_month_df <- dlh_temp_df %>%
  group_by(YEAR, MONTH) %>%
  summarize(
    YEARMODA = first(YEARMODA),
    TEMP = mean(TEMP, na.rm = TRUE)
  )


# Plot the monthly means ----------------------------------
month_temp_plot <- dlh_month_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = YEARMODA, y = TEMP)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Duluth Monthly Mean Temperature",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

month_temp_plot









Better — but still busy.

The seasonal cycle (summer peaks, winter dips) is now a clean, regular wave
A faint regression line is visible, but the seasonal swing still dominates the y-axis range

first(YEARMODA) keeps one representative date per month so we can still plot on a time axis.




Summarize by Year — The Story Gets Clear



# Mean temperature per year -------------------------------
dlh_year_df <- dlh_temp_df %>%
  group_by(YEAR) %>%
  summarize(
    YEARMODA = first(YEARMODA),
    TEMP = mean(TEMP, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

head(dlh_year_df)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
   YEAR YEARMODA    TEMP
  <int> <date>     <dbl>
1  1948 1948-01-01  3.76
2  1949 1949-01-01  4.10
3  1950 1950-01-01  1.60
4  1951 1951-01-01  2.41
5  1952 1952-01-01  4.55
6  1953 1953-01-01  4.55



yearly_temp_plot <- dlh_year_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = YEAR, y = TEMP)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "firebrick") +
  labs(
    title = "Duluth Annual Mean Temperature, 1948–2025",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Temp (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

yearly_temp_plot









Now the trend is obvious.

The seasonal noise is completely averaged out
78 points instead of 28,000 — and the story is clearer, not weaker
The blue/red trend line is the same kind of geom_smooth(method = "lm") line from Lecture 03

This is the power of group_by() %>% summarize(): the right level of summary reveals the signal.




Same Data, Three Levels — Side by Side





Level
What it shows
What it hides




Daily
every weather event
the long-term trend


Monthly
the seasonal cycle
day-to-day noise


Yearly
the climate trend
season, weather events



Key idea: there is no single “correct” level — it depends on your question. Want to know about a heat wave? Use daily. Want to know about climate change? Use yearly.







Important



Summarizing is not “losing information” — it’s choosing which question you’re answering.


📖 R4DS Ch. 3.5 — group_by() + summarize() workflow




🛑 Pause — Do Activity Parts 4–5 Now
Summarize the daily data to monthly and yearly means, and plot each. Predict how many rows each summary has, and what trend appears, before you run it.


🧩 Chunk 3 of 4 · Model the Rate of Change
We will cover: reusing lm(TEMP ~ YEAR) to estimate the warming slope, and converting it to °C per decade.






Tip



🖐 After this chunk: Activity Part 6 (fit the trend model and read the slope).




What Is the Rate of Change? — Reusing lm()






Note



🔮 Predict first: If Duluth is warming, will the slope of TEMP ~ YEAR be positive or negative? Guess the size too — closer to 0.02 or 2 °C per year?





# Fit a regression: TEMP predicted by YEAR ---------------
yearly_temp_model <- lm(TEMP ~ YEAR, data = dlh_year_df)

summary(yearly_temp_model)


Call:
lm(formula = TEMP ~ YEAR, data = dlh_year_df)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-1.99794 -0.51059  0.00688  0.49950  1.90458 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -49.096842   9.119103  -5.384 9.77e-07 ***
YEAR          0.026872   0.004585   5.860 1.49e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.8774 on 68 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3356,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3258 
F-statistic: 34.34 on 1 and 68 DF,  p-value: 1.489e-07



This is exactly Lecture 05’s lm() syntax — only now:

X = YEAR (instead of paper mass)
Y = TEMP (instead of paper area)
The slope is no longer “cm² per gram” — it’s °C per year

H₀: β = 0 (no warming trend)
Hₐ: β ≠ 0 (temperature is changing over time)




Extracting and Interpreting the Slope



# Pull the slope and convert to °C per decade ------------
yearly_intercept <- coef(yearly_temp_model)[1]
yearly_slope <- coef(yearly_temp_model)[2]

cat("Slope (b)         =", round(yearly_slope, 4), "°C/year\n")

Slope (b)         = 0.0269 °C/year

cat("Warming rate       =", round(yearly_slope * 10, 3), "°C per decade\n")

Warming rate       = 0.269 °C per decade



Why multiply by 10?

The raw slope is in °C per year — a small, hard-to-feel number
Multiplying by 10 converts to °C per decade — easier to communicate
This is the same coef() extraction skill from Lecture 05


b = 0.02 °C/year → 0.2 °C/decade — small year to year, but adds up over 78 years





Does the Same Pattern Hold at the Monthly Level?



# Fit the same model on the monthly summary ---------------
monthly_temp_model <- lm(TEMP ~ YEARMODA, data = dlh_month_df)

summary(monthly_temp_model)


Call:
lm(formula = TEMP ~ YEARMODA, data = dlh_month_df)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-23.285  -9.826   1.130  10.303  17.402 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 3.734e+00  4.954e-01   7.538 1.25e-13 ***
YEARMODA    7.788e-05  4.588e-05   1.698   0.0899 .  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 11.04 on 834 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.003444,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.002249 
F-statistic: 2.882 on 1 and 834 DF,  p-value: 0.08995



Compare to the yearly model:

Same overall warming direction
More residual scatter, because each point still carries some seasonal “memory”
The yearly summary gives the cleanest, most interpretable slope for a long-term trend question

This is why we chose the yearly summary for our headline result.




🛑 Pause — Do Activity Part 6 Now
Fit lm(TEMP ~ YEAR) on the yearly means, pull the slope, and convert it to °C per decade. Predict the sign and rough size before you run summary().


🧩 Chunk 4 of 4 · Seasons — Is Winter Warming Faster?
We will cover: building a season with case_when(), summarizing by year within season, plotting both, and fitting a separate lm() per season to compare rates.






Tip



🖐 After this chunk: Activity Parts 7–11 (season variable, per-season models, and the results paragraph).




A New Question — Is Every Season Warming the Same?


So far we’ve asked: is Duluth warming overall?
New question: is winter warming at the same rate as summer?
This matters biologically — earlier springs, shorter ice seasons, and changing growing seasons don’t depend on the annual average. They depend on which season is changing fastest.
Plan:

Label every day as summer or winter using case_when()
Summarize mean temperature by year within each season
Fit a separate lm() for each season
Compare the two slopes








Tip



🖐 Try it yourself
Make a prediction now: which season do you think is warming faster — winter or summer? We’ll find out with real data.






Building a Season Variable with case_when()






Note



🔮 Predict first: case_when() labels each day summer / winter / shoulder. Before the count() runs — which category will have the most rows, and why?





# Label each day as summer, winter, or shoulder season ----
dlh_season_df <- dlh_temp_df %>%
  mutate(
    season = case_when(
      MONTH %in% c(6, 7, 8) ~ "summer",
      MONTH %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "winter",
      TRUE ~ "shoulder"
    )
  )

# Quick check - did it work? -------------------------------
dlh_season_df %>%
  count(season)

     season     n
     <char> <int>
1: shoulder 12718
2:   summer  6436
3:   winter  6287



Reading case_when():

Each line is read top to bottom: condition ~ result
MONTH %in% c(6, 7, 8) — “is MONTH one of 6, 7, or 8?”
TRUE ~ "shoulder" — the catch-all for everything not matched above (spring/fall)

This is a new, more powerful cousin of the ifelse() you’ve used before — case_when() handles many conditions cleanly.
📖 R4DS Ch. 3.4 — case_when() for multi-way mutate()




Summarize Each Season by Year



# Keep only summer and winter, then summarize by year -----
season_year_df <- dlh_season_df %>%
  filter(season %in% c("summer", "winter")) %>%
  group_by(YEAR, season) %>%
  summarize(
    TEMP = mean(TEMP, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

head(season_year_df)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
# Groups:   YEAR [3]
   YEAR season  TEMP
  <int> <chr>  <dbl>
1  1948 summer  17.4
2  1948 winter -12.6
3  1949 summer  18.4
4  1949 winter -11.4
5  1950 summer  15.3
6  1950 winter -13.6



What changed:

filter() drops shoulder-season days — we only want the two extremes
group_by(YEAR, season) — grouping by two variables gives us one mean temperature per year per season

This produces a tidy long-format data frame — perfect for both plotting and modeling.




Plot Both Seasons Together



# Plot both seasons with separate trend lines --------------
season_temp_plot <- season_year_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = YEAR, y = TEMP, color = season)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "summer" = "firebrick",
      "winter" = "darkblue"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Duluth Summer vs. Winter Temperature Trends",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Temp (°C)",
    color = "Season"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

season_temp_plot









What to look for:

Two clearly separated bands — winter is much colder than summer, as expected
Compare the steepness of each trend line, not just the starting height
A steeper slope means a faster rate of warming for that season





Fit a Separate Model for Each Season






Note



🔮 Predict first: Commit now — which season warms faster in Duluth, summer or winter? Write your guess before the two slopes print.





# Summer-only model -----------------------------------------
summer_df <- season_year_df %>% filter(season == "summer")
summer_model <- lm(TEMP ~ YEAR, data = summer_df)
summer_slope <- coef(summer_model)[2]


# Winter-only model -----------------------------------------
winter_df <- season_year_df %>% filter(season == "winter")
winter_model <- lm(TEMP ~ YEAR, data = winter_df)
winter_slope <- coef(winter_model)[2]


cat("Summer warming rate:", round(summer_slope * 10, 3), "°C/decade\n")

Summer warming rate: 0.211 °C/decade

cat("Winter warming rate:", round(winter_slope * 10, 3), "°C/decade\n")

Winter warming rate: 0.342 °C/decade



Why fit two separate models instead of one model with season as a predictor?

Two simple models are easier to interpret at this stage
Each gives us a clean, separate slope (°C/decade) to directly compare

Spoiler from the climate science literature: in most northern locations, winter warms faster than summer — fewer extreme-cold days, shorter ice seasons. Does Duluth’s data agree?




🛑 Pause — Do Activity Parts 7–11 Now
Build the season variable, summarize and plot both seasons, fit a model for each, and write your results paragraph. Predict which season warms faster before you run the models.


What We Learned Today


Concepts:

Real climate data can be downloaded directly into R with GSODR
Raw daily data hides long-term trends inside seasonal/day-to-day noise
group_by() %>% summarize() at different time scales reveals different stories
The same lm() workflow from Lecture 05 works on any X ~ Y relationship — including time
case_when() builds a new categorical variable from multiple conditions
Splitting data by group (season) before modeling lets us compare rates of change

R skills:

get_GSOD() — download NOAA station data
group_by(YEAR, MONTH) / group_by(YEAR) — multi-level time summaries
case_when() — multi-condition mutate()
filter(x %in% c(...)) — keep only specific categories
Two-group regression comparison with separate lm() calls


References:

📖 R4DS Ch. 3 — Data transformation
📖 R4DS Ch. 17 — Dates and times
📖 Data Carpentry — R for Ecologists

Up next — Extension (out of class):

Pick your own city (anywhere with a long GSOD record)
Repeat the workflow: download → summarize → model the annual trend
Compare your city’s warming rate to Duluth’s, and predict first — by hand

title: Lecture 10 — T-Tests II: Running & Reporting the Test
text:
Where we left off (Lecture 09 — T-Tests I)

H₀: \(\mu_{shady} = \mu_{sunny}\) · Hₐ: \(\mu_{shady} \neq \mu_{sunny}\) (two-tailed, α = 0.05)
Normality checked — histogram + Shapiro-Wilk, roughly bell-shaped for ~25 per group
Variance checked — Levene’s test run (we use Welch’s either way)
Decision: proceed with Welch’s two-sample t-test







Note



✅ Key idea from Lecture 09
Every box is checked. Today we actually run the test, decode what R hands back, and turn it into a sentence a reader can trust.




Goals for Today



Run Welch’s two-sample t-test in R
Read every line of the t.test() output
Decide: reject or fail to reject H₀
Visualize the result with the test statistics embedded
Report results in proper scientific writing format







Tip



🖐 Try it yourself
By the end you will have a complete, reportable t-test result and a publication-style figure to go with it — whatever the test says.



References:

📖 Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 4 — Estimating with Uncertainty
📖 R4DS §3

Both are in the course readings/ folder.
Today’s naming:

test objects → _model
plots → _plot





How to Use These Slides — Predict · Type · Run


This lecture runs in two short chunks. After each chunk you switch to the activity and type the code yourself into your R script.
For every code block, do three things:

Predict — before it runs, say what you think the output will be
Type it out by hand — do not copy-paste
Run it and compare to your prediction








Note



✅ Why bother?
Guessing “above or below 0.05” before you see t.test() output forces you to reason about the test instead of just reading a number off the screen — that habit is what makes a p-value meaningful instead of magic.






Load Libraries and Data

# Load all packages at the top ----------------------------
library(readxl) # reading Excel files
library(tidyverse) # data manipulation + ggplot2
library(janitor) # clean_names()
library(car) # Levene's test for variance equality


# Load the leaf data from the data folder -----------------
leaf_df <- read_excel("data/2026_09_03_data_sci_leaf_area.xlsx") %>%
  clean_names()



Quick Recap of Our Assumption Checks



# Rerun the assumption checks quickly for reference -----
recap_df <- leaf_df %>%
  group_by(shade) %>%
  summarize(
    n = sum(!is.na(mass_g)),
    mean_mass = round(mean(mass_g, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    sd_mass = round(sd(mass_g, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    se_mass = round(sd_mass / sqrt(n), 3)
  )
recap_df

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  shade     n mean_mass sd_mass se_mass
  <chr> <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 shady    28     0.523   0.148   0.028
2 sunny    25     0.505   0.21    0.042

leveneTest(mass_g ~ shade, data = leaf_df)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
      Df F value  Pr(>F)  
group  1  2.9667 0.09105 .
      51                  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




Both groups: roughly normal (Lecture 09)
Levene’s: recorded, but does not change our test choice
We proceed with Welch’s (var.equal = FALSE)







Tip



If your Activity 09 numbers don’t match exactly, that’s fine — small rounding differences don’t change the conclusion.






🧩 Chunk 1 of 2 · Run & Interpret
We will cover: running Welch’s t.test(), reading every line of the output, and making a formal reject / fail-to-reject decision.

🛑 After this chunk: Activity Parts 1–3 (run, decode, decide).



Step 4 — Run the Welch’s t-Test






Note



🔮 Predict first: Write down a guess for the p-value before you run t.test() — above or below 0.05? Then see how close you were.





# Welch's two-sample t-test — unequal variance ---------
leaf_ttest_model <- t.test(
  mass_g ~ shade, # formula: response ~ grouping variable
  data = leaf_df,
  var.equal = FALSE, # Welch's — no pooled variance
  alternative = "two.sided" # two-tailed test
)

leaf_ttest_model


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  mass_g by shade
t = 0.35579, df = 42.527, p-value = 0.7238
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group shady and group sunny is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.08392774  0.11987117
sample estimates:
mean in group shady mean in group sunny 
          0.5230357           0.5050640 



Key arguments:







argument
what it does




mass_g ~ shade
compare mass_g between levels of shade


var.equal = FALSE
use Welch’s correction


alternative = "two.sided"
two-tailed test



The result is a model object. We decode each line of the output on the next slide.




Reading the t.test() Output



# Extract individual values from the model object ------
cat("t-statistic  :", round(leaf_ttest_model$statistic, 3), "\n")

t-statistic  : 0.356 

cat("df (Welch)   :", round(leaf_ttest_model$parameter, 2), "\n")

df (Welch)   : 42.53 

cat("p-value      :", signif(leaf_ttest_model$p.value, 3), "\n")

p-value      : 0.724 

cat(
  "95% CI       :",
  round(leaf_ttest_model$conf.int[1], 3),
  "to",
  round(leaf_ttest_model$conf.int[2], 3),
  "g\n"
)

95% CI       : -0.084 to 0.12 g

cat("Mean shady   :", round(leaf_ttest_model$estimate[1], 3), "g\n")

Mean shady   : 0.523 g

cat("Mean sunny   :", round(leaf_ttest_model$estimate[2], 3), "g\n")

Mean sunny   : 0.505 g



Line by line:







output
meaning




t
our calculated t-statistic


df
Welch-Satterthwaite df (non-integer is normal!)


p-value
probability of this result if H₀ is true


95% CI
plausible range for the true difference in means


mean of shady/sunny
the two group means



If the 95% CI includes zero, “no difference” is one of the plausible values — consistent with a p above 0.05.




Step 5 — Make a Decision



# State the decision formally --------------------------
# if/else: R checks the condition and runs one of two blocks
# We will learn these formally in the functions lecture
p_val <- leaf_ttest_model$p.value
alpha <- 0.05

if (p_val < alpha) {
  cat("p =", signif(p_val, 3), "< α =", alpha, "\n")
  cat("Decision: REJECT H₀\n")
  cat("Conclusion: mean leaf mass differs between sides.\n")
} else {
  cat("p =", signif(p_val, 3), ">= α =", alpha, "\n")
  cat("Decision: FAIL TO REJECT H₀\n")
  cat("Conclusion: no evidence that mean leaf mass differs between sides.\n")
}

p = 0.724 >= α = 0.05 
Decision: FAIL TO REJECT H₀
Conclusion: no evidence that mean leaf mass differs between sides.









Important



What the p-value means:
If H₀ were true (no real difference), we would get a t-statistic at least this large p × 100% of the time just by chance.
We set α = 0.05 before the test. If p < α, we reject H₀; otherwise we fail to reject it.


What “fail to reject” does NOT mean:

It is not proof that H₀ is true
It means this sample did not provide enough evidence of a difference
Report the effect size (difference in means) and CI alongside p





→ ACTIVITY 10 Parts 1–3 now

🛑 Do Activity Parts 1–3 now
Run the test, decode t / df / p / CI, and state your decision in formal language. Predict the p-value first.



🧩 Chunk 2 of 2 · Visualize & Report
We will cover: embedding the test result in a boxplot and writing a scientific results sentence.

🛑 After this chunk: Activity Parts 4–5 (plot and the results sentence).



Visualize the Result



# Final boxplot with all points -----------------------
leaf_box_10_plot <- leaf_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = shade, y = mass_g, fill = shade)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, seed = 42),
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Leaf Mass by Shade",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Welch's t-test: t = ",
      round(leaf_ttest_model$statistic, 2),
      ", p = ",
      signif(leaf_ttest_model$p.value, 2)
    ),
    x = "Shade",
    y = "Leaf Mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
leaf_box_10_plot









Including the test result in the figure:

subtitle pulls t and p directly from the model object
R fills in the actual numbers automatically
If you re-run with new data, the subtitle updates







Tip



Embedding test statistics in the plot subtitle saves you from copying numbers by hand — and avoids typos in your report.






How to Report Results in Science



# Build the results sentence from the model object -----
t_val  <- round(leaf_ttest_model$statistic, 2)
df_val <- round(leaf_ttest_model$parameter, 1)
p_val2 <- signif(leaf_ttest_model$p.value, 2)

heavier <- if (leaf_ttest_model$estimate[1] > leaf_ttest_model$estimate[2]) "shady" else "sunny"
lighter <- if (heavier == "shady") "sunny" else "shady"

cat("--- Results sentence ---\n")

--- Results sentence ---

if (leaf_ttest_model$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(heavier, "-side leaves were significantly heavier than ",
      lighter, "-side leaves\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("Mean leaf mass did not differ significantly between sides\n")
}

Mean leaf mass did not differ significantly between sides

cat("(Welch's t-test: t(", df_val, ") = ", t_val, ", p = ", p_val2, ").\n", sep = "")

(Welch's t-test: t(42.5) = 0.36, p = 0.72).

cat(
  "Mean ± SE: shady =",
  round(leaf_ttest_model$estimate[1], 3),
  "±",
  round(recap_df$se_mass[recap_df$shade == "shady"], 3),
  "g,  sunny =",
  round(leaf_ttest_model$estimate[2], 3),
  "±",
  round(recap_df$se_mass[recap_df$shade == "sunny"], 3),
  "g.\n"
)

Mean ± SE: shady = 0.523 ± 0.028 g,  sunny = 0.505 ± 0.042 g.



Standard format:

“[Finding] (Welch’s t-test: t(df) = X.XX, p = X.XXX; mean ± SE: group1 = X.X ± X.X units, group2 = X.X ± X.X units).”

Always include:

Test type (Welch’s t-test)
t-statistic and df
Exact p-value (or < 0.001)
Group means ± SE with units

A non-significant result is still a result — report it plainly (“did not differ significantly”), never as “proved there is no difference.”
Never report “p = 0.000” — write “p < 0.001” instead.




Save Your Plot

# Save the plot to the figures folder ------------------
ggsave(
  "figures/leaf_mass_boxplot_ttest.png",
  plot = leaf_box_10_plot,
  width = 5,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)



Your plot is now in your figures/ folder with the test statistics embedded in the subtitle — ready for a lab report or paper.







Tip



dpi = 300 is publication quality. Use it for any figure that will appear in a paper, poster, or formal report.

Build the figure with the statistics embedded in the subtitle, then write your results sentence. Predict what the subtitle will say before you run it.



What We Learned Today


Concepts:

Steps 4–5 of the five-step framework — run, interpret, report
Reading output — t, df, p, CI, group means
A results sentence needs: test name, t, df, p, means ± SE, units
A non-significant result is reported plainly — not as proof of “no difference”

R skills:

t.test(y ~ group, data, var.equal = FALSE, alternative = "two.sided")
model$statistic, model$p.value, model$conf.int — extract results
paste0(...) in labs(subtitle = ) — embed test statistics in figures

📖 Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 4 — Estimating with Uncertainty
📖 R4DS §3
